newsitem.title: ZAIRE: Thousands more refugees head back into Rwanda.
newsitem.headline: Thousands more refugees head back into Rwanda.

text.p: Tens of thousands of Rwandan Hutu refugees streamed home across the border from Zaire on Saturday for the second straight day, witnesses said.
"The road of death is now a road of hope," said Ray Wilkinson of the U.N. refugee agency, UNHCR, adding the returnees were in good shape physically and seemed cheerful.
Witnesses said the road leading west into Zaire, where the Hutus fled in panic after Tutsis won power in 1994, was packed with people, carrying all their possessions.
"It is an incredible sight, a moving sea of people," reported one journalist.
The UNHCR said some 300,000 people had converged on the east Zairean town of Goma and were now moving towards the border. They were crossing at the rate of 12,000 an hour.
"Some 100,000 have crossed since yesterday, they are so many we cannot register them," UNHCR spokesman Peter Kessler said.
The returnees were massing at the Nkamira transit camp and would be transported to their home districts by trucks and buses later on Saturday.
"We have 50 trucks already, another 20 on the way, and are organising 100 more buses and trucks in Kigali," Kessler said.

The refugees began returning home on Friday after a six-hour bombardment broke the hold over them of Hutu gunmen, members of the ex-Rwandan army and militia groups wanted for the 1994 genocide of up to one million people, mostly Tutsis.

But the humanitarian crisis, brought to a head by last month's revolt of Zairean rebels, looked far from solved as many more refugees were scattered across eastern Zaire and the region remained a potential war zone.
The revolt in eastern Zaire, which groups ethnic Tutsis and other opponents of ailing President Mobutu Sese Seko, has also put hundreds of thousands of Zaireans to flight.

The Hutu returnees had been held virtual hostage in the huge Mugunga camp, intimidated into staying in exile, until Zairean rebels bombarded it on Thursday. The Hutu militiamen were reported to have fled into the bush.
The refugees left behind mutilated corpses of a handful of men, women and children and a mystery as to how they died.

To the west, witnesses spoke of fighting between Zairean rebels and fleeing Hutu hardliners. They said a plane overflying the area had been fired on by anti-aircraft guns early on Saturday, but was not hit.
Reporters saw 13 more bodies in a ditch by the road to Goma. One woman had been decapitated and had her limbs cut off. She lay in a tangle of bodies and belongings.
Some refugees said Tutsi rebels had killed the refugees but this could not be independently confirmed. Others said Hutu hardliners had previously intimidated refugees into staying.
The return of the refugees offered some hope to the crisis in central Africa, but the United Nations still voted to dispatch a multinational humanitarian force.
The 15-member U.N. Security Council on Friday unanimously approved the deployment of the Canadian-led multinational force until March 31 to ensure food and medicine reached refugees.

Over a million Hutus fled Rwanda fearing reprisals after the 1994 genocide and a civil war in which an army dominated by returning Tutsi exiles took power. Hundreds of thousands of Hutus fled from an equally bitter civil war in Burundi.
